lead: A Poisson process counts events that arrive one at a time, independently, at a constant average rate. It answers questions such as how many UPI requests hit a server in the next minute, or how long until the next bus. The count in an interval has a Poisson distribution, and the gaps between events have an exponential distribution. A renewal process keeps the independent-gap idea but allows any gap law. These models feed queueing, reliability and the continuous-time Markov chains of 7.6.
prereq: You need: the Poisson and exponential distributions from Unit 3; 7.1 for the idea of a random process.

blocks.text: A Poisson process models events that arrive one at a time, independently, at a constant average rate. Write N(t) for the number of events in the time interval [0,t]. The rate is λ events per unit time. For example, λ=0.5 per hour means half a call per hour on average.

The process has three defining properties. N(0)=0. Counts in disjoint time intervals are independent (independent increments). The count in any interval of length t has the same distribution wherever the interval sits (stationary increments).

blocks.where: N(t) is the count by time t; λ is the rate per unit time; e is 2.718...; k! = 1×2×...×k. The mean and variance are both λt.

blocks.text: Mean and variance equal λt. A Poisson count therefore has spread equal to its average. Over 6 hours at λ=0.5 per hour, N(6) has mean 3 and variance 3. Some syllabi call the Poisson process a pure birth process because the count only goes up by one.

Let T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, ... be the gaps between successive events. For a Poisson process these interarrival times are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables with mean 1/λ. The exponential distribution is memoryless: after a wait, the remaining wait has the same distribution (see Unit 3, Exponential distribution and the memoryless property).

blocks.where: T is one interarrival time; λ is the rate per unit time; the mean is 1/λ and the variance is 1/λ².

blocks.text: The k-th arrival time S<sub>k</sub> = T<sub>1</sub> + ... + T<sub>k</sub> is gamma (Erlang) with shape k and rate λ. Its mean is k/λ. The first three arrival times in the figure are 2 h, 6 h and 7 h.

items: Merging: if two independent Poisson processes have rates λ<sub>1</sub> and λ<sub>2</sub>, their combined events form a Poisson process with rate λ<sub>1</sub>+λ<sub>2</sub>.
Thinning: if each event is kept independently with probability p, the kept events form a Poisson process with rate λp.

blocks.text: These two rules let you split or combine call streams. A help desk with two independent call types can be analysed as one stream, or one stream can be split by type.

sections.h3: Renewal processes: the same idea with any gap law

blocks.text: A renewal process keeps the independent interarrival idea but drops the exponential requirement. The interarrival times T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub>, ... are iid with mean μ and variance σ². N(t) still counts events by time t. The process renews after every event.
The renewal function is m(t)=E[N(t)], the expected number of renewals by time t. For a Poisson process μ=1/λ and m(t)=λt exactly. For general interarrival laws m(t) is not simply t/μ at small t.

blocks.where: m(t) is the expected count by time t; μ is the mean interarrival time; the limit is the elementary renewal theorem. The long-run renewal rate is 1/μ events per unit time.

blocks.text: Use renewal models for machine replacement, warranty claims and repairable systems. The exponential case is the Poisson process; other gap laws give the same long-run rate but different short-run behaviour. Continuous-time Markov chains in 7.6 use exponential sojourns, so the Poisson process is their simplest counting example.

figure.caption: The first three interarrival times of the help desk example: 2 h, 4 h and 1 h. The arrival times are the ends of the bars, at 2 h, 6 h and 7 h.

spec.aria: A timeline shows three interarrival intervals of 2 hours, 4 hours and 1 hour, ending at 7 hours.

examples.question: A help desk receives calls as a Poisson process with rate λ=0.5 per hour. (a) Find the probability of no call in 2 hours. (b) Find the mean and variance of the number of calls in 6 hours. (c) The first three interarrival times are 2 h, 4 h and 1 h; find the first three arrival times.
steps: Write λ=0.5 h⁻¹. For an interval of length t, N(t) is Poisson with mean λt.
(b) t=6 h, so λt=0.5×6=3. For a Poisson random variable mean=λt=3 and variance=λt=3.
(c) Arrival times are cumulative sums. S<sub>1</sub>=2 h. S<sub>2</sub>=2+4=6 h. S<sub>3</sub>=6+1=7 h.
examples.answer: The probability of no call in 2 hours is 0.3679; in 6 hours the mean and variance are both 3 calls; the first three arrival times are 2 h, 6 h and 7 h.

traps: Do not use e<sup>−λt</sup> for the count probability when k>0; use e<sup>−λt</sup>(λt)<sup>k</sup>/k!.
The exponential formula gives waiting time, not count. P(T>t)=e<sup>−λt</sup> is for the gap, not P(N(t)=k).
Use the interval length in λt. A rate of 0.5 per hour over 30 minutes gives λt=0.25, not 0.5.
Mean and variance of a Poisson count are equal. If a question asks for standard deviation, take √(λt).
In a renewal process with non-exponential gaps, m(t) is not λt. Only the long-run rate 1/μ is simple.

quiz.q: Define the Poisson process N(t) with rate λ. State N(0) and the pmf of N(t).
quiz.a: N(t) counts events by time t; N(0)=0; independent and stationary increments; P(N(t)=k)=e<sup>−λt</sup>(λt)<sup>k</sup>/k! for k=0,1,2,...

quiz.q: Why are the mean and variance of N(t) both λt?
quiz.a: The Poisson pmf gives E[N(t)]=Var[N(t)]=λt. Equivalently, independent increments add both means and variances at rate λ per unit time.

quiz.q: Calls arrive as a Poisson process with λ=2 per hour. Find P(no call in 3 hours).
For a Poisson process with λ=0.25 per minute, find the mean interarrival time in minutes.
Two independent Poisson streams have rates 2 and 3 per hour. What is the rate of the merged stream?
quiz.a: By merging, rates add: 2+3=5 per hour.

quiz.q: A Poisson stream has rate 10 per hour. Each event is kept with probability 0.2. What is the rate of kept events?
quiz.a: By thinning, the kept rate is λp=10×0.2=2 per hour.

quiz.q: State one difference between a Poisson process and a general renewal process.
quiz.a: A Poisson process has iid exponential gaps; a renewal process allows any iid gap law with mean μ. For Poisson m(t)=λt exactly; for a general renewal only m(t)/t→1/μ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Renewal theory underpins reliability engineering, queueing analysis and warranty costing. Search for 'renewal reward theorem' to see how long-run cost per unit time is computed. Non-homogeneous Poisson processes let λ vary with time; search 'non-homogeneous Poisson process'. In industry, Poisson models size telephony call arrivals and server requests; renewal models handle wear-out and repair. These ideas lead to queueing theory and to the continuous-time Markov chains in 7.6.
